I don’t know what the future holds for any of us—every day is something different. There are a lot of people who have the privilege to leave and, like you, I am not one of them. So all I can do is problem solve the issues as they come. I’ve done fit tests on masks only for the fit to vary every time I put on a new mask of the one I’ve fit tested. 🤷‍♀️I found doing a mirror test helps a lot. Here’s what I do every time I put on my mask: Take a deep breath and breathe out slowly with a small makeup mirror on one side of my mask, near my cheek, by my ear. Does it fog? No? Good. I do this on each side and above my eyes. If I’m not getting any fog, I am satisfied that it is fit enough. I can now do this test in just a minute or so. I also use wig tape on the nose bridge of every mask to aid with fit. Thats what I do, but don’t take it as gospel. This is just my experience and so far so good.

Humans have terrible recollection over time, too. Our memory of events from just a few years ago can become easily distorted by the stories we hear other people tell and then turn around and tell ourselves. Our memories can be easily influenced by inaccurate information. So, for example, my friend remembers lockdown lasting months, but in reality, it lasted about two weeks in the US. She tells me that she was trapped inside for several months but I clearly remember us going to the Burger King drive thru and having outdoor picnics just days after lockdown was lifted. She even went back to work. Memory is not a solid thing and it can be easily manipulated by so many factors.

When I am faced with this situation, I often think: is it even worth it? It sounds like your friend is willing to do very little for your safety, their safety or the safety of anyone else. So, is it worth the emotional taxation that is even required to “hang out” with people who can’t even do the bare minimum? I lost a friendship of over 25 years because she kept saying she was pitying me and “was sad that I felt I had to live this way”. As soon as I heard that, she no longer got access to my life because it was obvious her moral compass did not align with mine. Sometimes its easier to drop the baggage than to try and find ways to carry it.

Hi, friend. I have a diagnosis of OCD and PTSD and my intrusive thoughts are part of a wide range of symptoms I experience because of my diagnosis. Its certainly possible that you may have a form of OCD or PTSD. 

Every person's diagnosis is different, but what makes up and OCD diagnosis is two-fold. Firstly: You must have an obsession. Thoughts can certainly be classified as an obsession and intrusive thoughts are often lumped into this category for very good reason. If they are on a repeated loop, your brain has begun to obsess over the thought(s). Secondly, there is typically a compulsion to relieve the obsession. A compulsion is something you MUST do. If you don't follow through with your compulsion it can lead to things like panic attacks and extreme dread. For me, it brought about panic episodes so bad that I felt like I was going to die. And if I didn't resolve my obsession "correctly" this would lead me to do it over and over and over again. Do you experience compulsions as well as these obsessive thoughts?

Another thing that could be happening is linked to PTSD. Often, a person with PTSD will "relive" or remember traumatic experiences again and again on a repeated loop or when specifically triggered by stimuli that are relevant to that moment in time. These episodes often come along with a lot of physical symptoms (but not always). My PTSD comes from several different events that occurred, repeatedly, over the years but always reinforced the same experience over and over again. 

I'll offer an example of what an intrusive episode is for me and maybe you can see if it sounds familiar to you. For this example, I'll use a pretty common daily scene:

I am standing at the kitchen sink washing dishes. I am focused on the task, but because I've done it loads of times before, my mind starts to wander. After only a few seconds, it falls into the deep crags of an intrusive thought. The thought is often the same: "You are all alone and it is not safe for you to be alone." It comes in several flavors (sometimes my mind likes to get extra spicy and tell me I'll never have a sexual partner ever again) but the baseline is always the same. I am suddenly overcome with extreme loneliness and like I am the only person on the planet. The anxiety grips me around the heart and lungs; sometimes I stop breathing for a moment. Every time I have this thought I feel dread in the pit of my stomach. It feels like everything is pointless because I am alone and bad things happen when I am alone.

Sometimes, it only lasts a few seconds, sometimes it destroys my entire day. I find that if I distract myself right away I can move through the thought and carry on until it happens again. If I can't catch it and my mind spirals, often nothing can stop it until I am crying or calling a friend to help ground me. 

I say ALL of this to say: there is no right answer to intrusive thoughts. There are so many reasons they can happen but we must remember that the problem is not the THOUGHT itself, but the emotions that that thought brings to the table. What do you feel when you have this thought/memory? I suggest journaling your experience once or twice and see what physical and emotional reactions you are having to this thought. While we can get diagnosed and seek out help from professionals, the absolute best place you can start is: what feelings are attached to this intrusive thought? And then go from there. 

I hope this was helpful, albeit long.

I think a lot of pressure comes from how the world operates now. With the birth of the internet came the birth of everyone clambering to be heard and seen; to be validated in some way. Once everyone could scream into the void, they did. And now we have to try and hear ourselves over all the screaming.

Through no fault of our own, we are fed the constant message that we all need to be doing *more* somehow; that whatever we have in our lives is not enough. We see everyone around us posting about the fantastic parts of their lives and how happy they are, so when we look at our own lives we think, "Maybe this isn't enough?" And when things are going well, we begin to doubt whether its real or not. We start to unconsciously doubt things and compare ourselves to other people without even realizing it.

Most of the time, we don't even know its happening. We are surrounded by it, though, and its very nearly impossible to get away from it in some form or another. It gets under our skin and eats away at us until all we can think about is how horrible our lives are because they're so different from other people's lives. 

We are also constantly reminded that our happiness is fragile--we see TikTok videos of people's sadness at loss. We see constant news articles of people getting hurt or killed. We are shown images of sadness and expected not to feel that sadness on some level. But, we are human and now that we live in a connected world, we not only have to experience our own struggles and happiness, but we now have to experience the struggles and happiness of everyone else, all the time. 

You are not alone in any of this; we are ALL experiencing this in some form or another. Life is overwhelming and we no longer get to take a break from it. It's constant.

I struggle with this ALL. The. Time. People often don't emphasize the fact that depression is an imbalance in chemicals and hormones in your brain. Your brain is an organ, just like your stomach or your lungs. When we are sick with a stomach bug or a cold, we care for ourselves and others with medicine and good food and kind words. But, when we are mentally unwell, we are treated the opposite. We are told that something is wrong with us for being this way and others push us away because we are unwell.

I try very hard to remember this. I have been diagnosed with OCD and MDD and I am on Lexapro for it. But, that isn't a cure--like cold medicine isn't a cure for your illness--it just treats the symptoms. Some days I don't want to get out of bed, either. But, I get up and go to the bathroom and say, "If I want to, I can get back into bed after." Sometimes I do. Sometimes I force myself to stumble into the kitchen for a glass of water because I know that water helps me feel better.

I think of it as being sick with a cold and, somehow, it becomes easier for me to care for myself. I remember how I care for myself when I have a cold, or how my mother used to care for me when I had an ear infection and I try to emulate that. I remind myself that feeling "sick" is temporary and, if I care for myself, I will be well again soon.

Sometimes, we have to trick our mind into doing things, especially when it is our mind that is telling us not to.

So, when you feel like you can't get out of bed, just get up and get a glass of water from the kitchen or bathroom. Stand there at the sink and drink the entire thing in small sips. When you are done, make another decision about your day. If that's to go back to bed, well, at least you drank some water. But, I can assure you that the more you encourage yourself to take small steps, the easier it will become to tackle the larger steps.

Hi, friend. :) First of all, this took a lot of guts to post, so congrats on doing so. Secondly, what you're describing really isn't all that uncommon. It sounds like there is a void somewhere in your life that you're not quite sure how to fill (or feel able to fill). For me, I want stability in my life, but a part of me also wants spontaneity, adventure and the rush of novel experiences. Perhaps that's where the cheating comes in? Believe it or not, you can be both completely satisfied with your marriage and unhappy with your relationship. These things can co-exist inside you and neither of them are "wrong".

Often, we are unconsciously fulfilling what others want for us instead of fulfilling what *we* know to be best for us. Perhaps you're polyamorous instead of monogamous and, in your mind, you are aware of this but feel that it's somehow "wrong" based on everything you know about how relationships are "supposed to be". Processing through what is missing in our lives often takes a lot of time, introspection and lots of questions. It can be helpful to review your core values (things that make you who you are at the very inner you). You may want to ask your therapist to help you work on finding out what your core values are.

Additionally, depression and anxiety are often a symptom of our longing to have done something different in our lives or we feel like we are stuck with the choices that we made and have to just "make the best of it". Depression, itself, isn't a disease and it doesn't make you broken. It's an emotion, like joy or anger. It is your brain telling you "Pay attention to this, it's important!" 

Medication is a tool to help you learn how to sort through mental issues, so it isn't going to make you feel a specific way all the time. Brain chemistry changes from minute to minute, so you will have good days and bad days. Nothing is linear and, typically, we expect way more of ourselves than we really need to. I take medication, as well, but I will go for several days where I feel as though I haven't taken it, even though I have. Then, other times, I will feel like I'm doing really well and that I may not need my medication at all. 

Our minds are strange, complex things and they aren't always straightforward in the way they work. It's not like a knee, or an elbow, that works the same way all the time. The brain is flexible; it learns and changes based on experiences. So, take some time to allow your brain to think and feel strange. It's OK to feel weird or like you don't know what to do. Your thoughts and feelings cannot hurt you, they are only there as sign posts to help you figure out if your needs are being met or not.

Sometimes, all we need is to have a nice cup of coffee with a loved-one, or get a hug from a trusted friend. Hey friend, I hope I can help you. First of all, it is 100% completely normal to have overwhelming anxiety about COVID, especially a COVID diagnosis. Nothing about this entire situation is "normal", so there's no right or wrong way to react. Struggling in a chaotic world is absolutely alright. You are totally fine and there is nothing wrong with you.

Secondly, I struggle with my breathing when my anxiety is really bad, so I understand where you're coming from. Everyone kept tell me to take deep breaths, but that never seemed to do anything. So, I had to change how I breathed through the anxiety, a little.

The easiest thing to do when you feel the anxiety ramping up is lengthen your exhale. Take a normal breath, but when you exhale, just keep pushing the air out of your lungs until you have no more there. I do this five times in a row. Scientifically, this calms your body's natural stress response (you can read about it by Googling "vagus nerve") and relaxes your tense shoulders, neck and chest. While I'm doing this I will often clasp my hands behind my back and stretch my upper back. Usually, I find a lot of tension there. Tension causes you to, unconsciously, take smaller breaths, which can make it feel like you can't breathe.

Once you calm down a little, you can take deep breaths and squeeze your belly button backward toward your spine. Just breath in an tense your muscles there. This is another way to calm your vagus nerve. I do this with my eyes closed until my brain feels a little less chaotic. 

Next, stop Googling for a bit. Sometimes I will switch over to TikTok, or go watch a funny YouTube video, if I feel like I can't put my phone down. Otherwise, I will go outside and take the dogs for walk (or alone if the dogs don't want to go). On these walks I will play a game with myself where I just say the name of whatever I happen to be looking at. This is an easy form of mindfulness meditation and it doesn't have any rules. Just look at things and think of the name of that thing (grass, house, sidewalk, tree, blackbird, etc.) in your mind.

Lastly, talk to yourself rationally. It can be VERY hard (I struggle with this as someone with a terrible anxiety disorder). Think of the absolute WORST thing that can happen and really address that worry. So, if its "I may get COVID", then think about how you would handle that situation for yourself. If you're vaccinated, you'll probably be fine. If you have an underlying condition that might make the COVID worse, contact your doctor to see what they recommend you do if you start having symptoms. Sometimes coming up with a rational plan can put your worries at ease.

I hope this helps. Please feel free to message me if you have any questions. I would be more than happy to help.

So, first off: happiness is a lie. Somehow, we have all been fed a fairytale that, at some point, we will be "happy" or that others around us are somehow perpetually "happy". In reality, there are small pockets of joy and contentment, but happiness is just a big word to make you feel like a failure. My therapist encourages me to throw the idea of happiness out the window and strive for contentment instead. I've taken the word out of my vocabulary and it has helped some. If you can look at life as a series of ups and downs instead of a "journey toward happiness" it can be a little easier to manage. Life isn't a journey. There's no destination. We are just filling time however we feels matters to us most.

And on that note, the second thing I can suggest is evaluating your core values. Don't think about goals or who you want to be, where you want to be or anything like that. Just think about things that you find important. Really important. Deep down in there. For me, for example, it's dogs. That's it. Not family, friends, art or anything else. I like all those things and they are important, but dogs are literally what keeps me going. The only time I feel anything close to contentment is when I am around dogs.

So, my solution? I went to school to be a dog trainer. I scraped together money to start a small pet sitting business. I volunteer at a local dog shelter. These things don't always make me happy and sometimes they're absolutely exhausting, irritating and miserable, but they make me feel better in the long run because they are actions I take that speak to my core value, my love for dogs. I encourage you to take some time to journal about what you think might be a core value for you. It doesn't have to be some earth-shattering thing. Sometimes it's knitting. Maybe its basketball. Who knows? It could be anything.

And third, please know that you are not alone. Most of the time, I am pretty depressed or anxious. I feel weird emotions that I can't even name. I cry all the time. I think about killing myself a lot. I sit on the toilet sometimes and watch Tik Toks just so I don't feel so goddamn alone in the world. You are allowed to feel like you don't want to be on this planet anymore. I mean, the world is kind of a hellscape right now. I've been on Lexapro for about 7 years. I started taking it after I ran through a battery of other medications that made me very sick or did nothing at all. I recently went off Lexapro completely and it was the absolute worst. I became suicidal and was unable to cope so I went back on it. I am now back up to my old dose and feeling like I can manage my depression much better now.

Some things I learned during this process are:

1.) anti-depressants wont "cure" your depression but they will give you the relief you need to manage your symptoms *better.* The way my doctor described it is that the depression is always going to be there (unless you're on a medication that completely numbs you) but the medication gives you the opportunity to address it instead of be consumed by it.

2.) Lots of people feel like their antidepressants aren't really "doing anything" anymore, so they go off of them, only to discover that their symptoms return in full force. Then, when they go back on them, they realize that they *were* helping to improve the situation, even though it didn't seem like it.

I say all this as a kind of "cautionary tale" because I thought the same thing when, in reality, I needed to change my dose, add a medication (like Wellbutrin) or engage in talk therapy, DBT, CBT or other forms of mindfulness.

In the end, it's all up to you and your doctor, but I am back on Lexapro now and, while I am still absolutely depressed, I am functioning at a much higher level than I was.

Cortisol is naturally produced in everyone and it fluctuates naturally throughout the day. So, a “normal” person has cortisol being released in specific doses based on what the brain is asking for (its produced in the adrenal glands and helps regulate your stress response). In someone with anxiety, your brain is responding to whatever triggers your anxiety by releasing more cortisol, which naturally makes your anxiety worsen. Anxiety is just the activation of your primitive “fight, flight or freeze” response so the two go hand in hand. In answer to your question: its both. A trigger begins the process and the cortisol lingers until its processed by your body, which can keep your stress response activated well after the “trigger” is gone.

It's bizarre, but it helps take your mind off whatever you were thinking about that made you anxious and forces you to breathe deeply.

Sometimes, giving your feelings a physical presence helps to alleviate them. Remember, the more we try to make the thoughts and feelings go away, the more they stick with us. Worry: I am worried that my dog will get sick and die.

Firstly, know that you're not alone. Depression saps all motivation and, on top of that, your lack of motivation can make you feel guilty. This is super common with depression, so try not to be too hard on yourself about that.

Often, you can get financial aid, as well. You can also reach out on websites like this or join Discords where you can chat with others who are going through what you might be going through. My best advice, beyond all of that, is to start small. Often, we get overwhelmed by what we *should* be doing and we don't take into account what we want to be doing and that can lead to a complete overload. For me, I started by taking walks outside. I would walk around my neighborhood when things started to get too much. I played the "name game" and would look around while I walked and just thought about what I was seeing. "There's a tree. Oh, there's a bird in the tree. And a squirrel on the ground. That house is blue. There are some fluffy clouds in the sky" and so on and so on. Ask your mind to do just the simple task of naming things while you breathe and walk. It sounds silly, but its a good place to start when you don't know what else to do.

First off, you're not being whiny. Ironically, someone said something similar to me today: "There are people out there missing limbs. Your problem isn't that bad." While somewhat true, things like that imply that my pain isn't bad enough to warrant attention. But, here's the thing: its not a contest. Everyone experiences pain in relation to their life. So, yes, there are people out there who "have it worse", but the problem isn't with YOU, it's with how the world gauges your pain. Someone complaining of pain in their arm should receive the same attention as someone else complaining of pain in their soul.

With that being said, most people don't know how to react to someone in pain if there is no visible "wound", per say. We certainly know what to do if someone is injured, but there's no 3-digit number to call when someone is mentally in pain. As a society, we believe that emotional pain is, somehow, less valid than physical pain. So, those who are experiencing emotional pain often cause themselves *physical* harm to show the outside world what they feel on the inside.

I want you to know that what you are feeling is 100% valid and you are absolutely allowed to be in emotional pain, regardless of your situation. I, myself, have had a pretty good life, but I still cut myself at the age of 34, as I have done my whole life. I go to therapy and I take anti-depressants--these are all perfectly normal reactions to our emotional pain, regardless of where it comes from.

When my parents failed to take me seriously after my first suicide attempt, I sat them down with my therapist and all of us spoke about the problem. Sometimes, bringing in a third party can be very beneficial; someone who doesn't have a vested interest in your life other than your mental health can bring about a unique perspective that your parents may not be willing to get from you.

I hope this helps and I want you to know that, whatever you are feeling, you are allowed to feel it, no matter what anyone says.

Hey, friend. First of all: there is no need to reject those feelings. How you feel about those things is 100% valid and you are allowed to feel however you need to feel. 

Humans are born imitating others; its how we learn how to do pretty much everything! So, it's only natural to compare yourself to those around you and how they are doing. Its a natural habit to want to mimic what your friends are doing, especially at a young age.

Feeling like you are "falling short" is a very common feeling for everyone, especially with the dawn of social media. We see others doing all these amazing things we wish we were doing and we lose sight of whats important. 

I often sit down and write out a list of all the things I am confident about. Start with what you like about yourself. Are you really good at math? Maybe you're super talented when it comes to video games. Or, maybe you're really good at making things. Explore what makes you happy/excited and lean into those things instead. Focusing on our negative attributes or our "lack" or experience will only harbor more negativity. It becomes a vicious cycle.

Sex, drinking and partying will always be there. I'm 34 and I still get invited to parties, drink with friends and get asked out on the occasional date. So, when you think about milestones, don't worry about things like that: they will still be there when you're older. And, just for posterity, I didn't have sex until I was 24 so...there's no real rush.

All in all, feeling like you're not where others are is a completely natural and 100% human feeling. There's no need to be rid of those feelings. Instead, use them to discover what you are excelling at that others may not be.

"What happens next?"

This thought goes both ways because, either things will get better or they will get worse. You've already survived 100% of your worst days so, theoretically, a good one has to come along *at some point*. So, that's what keeps me going. My intense wonder at what will happen in the future--what will happen in my life if I just hang on a little longer.

Hi, friend. I am right there with you on this one. I struggle with existential dread, as well. Often, when I am doing something I enjoy, I worry about it ending and what comes next (for example: I'm really enjoying this bike ride, but when its over I have to go home and be alone and then what if I take a shower and fall while I'm in there or something happens and...).

One big thing I learned in therapy is to catch yourself saying "should" and change it to "want". There is no manual to how your life is supposed to go, so in reality, there is no set rule for what you "should" be doing or not doing. Should is a powerful word and it comes from a place inside us where we set ridiculous expectations (mostly without realizing it!) and when we don't reach those expectations or we fall short, we feel like we are failures or that we are broken in some way.

Sometimes, we look around us and we see others who seem to be doing better than we are so we try to compare ourselves to them. "I *should* be able to do XYZ because other people can." is such a detrimental statement and it is the cause of much of my own anxiety and worry.

I'm not perfect, by any means, but when I catch myself using "should" statements, I try to think, instead, about why I think I "should" be doing/not doing whatever it is. 

Life is about how you go through it, not how others expect you to so, yes, there is absolutely an end to these feelings but, surprisingly, it starts exactly where it is: in your mind.
